title: Cashing in on SpaceX: 'Every chance I get, I'll sell a little more'
description: Andre Lavoie joined SpaceX in 2009 as an engineer, designing the pressure tanks that help power its rocket. He was paid partly in stock - a common tra
body: Andre Lavoie joined SpaceX in 2009 as an engineer, designing the pressure tanks that help power its rocket. He was paid partly in stock - a common trade-off at start-ups as a hiring incentive.Some 17 years on, those 200,000 shares he was given are worth about $23m (£17m) - and the 63-year-old says he's ready to start cashing them as soon as he can."Every chance I get going forward, I'll sell a little bit more," he tells the BBC. "The shares have been going up so radically it keeps messing up my life plans - you really can't know the future, so it's better to sell early and in intervals."Lavoie is far from being the only one who has seen the value of his stake in SpaceX rocket over the years. The company's founder, Elon Musk, said on Fox News that SpaceX's listing on the stock market in June had likely made "several thousand" employees millionaires - including staff "who were working on the production line".According to reports, there are estimated to be 4,400 new millionaires created by the listing.Unlike most newly-listed firms, SpaceX shares are set to be released in stages: the first 20% on 6 August, with more due in batches through the rest of the year.Whether or not shareholders decide to sell their stake at the first opportunity is a matter for individuals. Unlike Lavoie, some may choose to hold onto their shares altogether in the hope of bigger gains later.SpaceX listed on the Nasdaq in June, in the biggest initial public offering (IPO) in history, valuing the rocket and satellite firm at more than $2 trillion. It briefly made Elon Musk the world's first trillionaire, before the stock cooled and his fortune slipped back below the milestone within weeks.In its first results as a public company this week, the firm's quarterly revenue was shown to have nearly doubled to $7.8bn (£5.8bn) from a year earlier, while its spending ballooned to $18.3bn - more than six times what it was a year ago.Overall, SpaceX made a net loss of $143m in the three months to June, and a loss of $2bn during the first six months of the year.Musk pushed back against sceptics on an earnings call: "I think people are really underestimating Starlink". He predicted the satellite internet service - the one part of the company that is currently making a profit - could one day deliver a majority of the world's internet.But shares in the company tumbled on the back of the earnings report, with investors generally spooked by the huge amounts of money being spent on AI.SpaceX shares fell 13.6% on Wednesday to $108.27 (£80.44) - well below the initial listing price of $135 a share.Lavoie plans to use his money from selling some of his shares to fund a hotel he is renovating in Pontebba, Italy's northeastern Friuli region, plus a small brewery.He says is priority for the future is raising awareness of air pollution in the area, in partnership with a local environmental group.Before he was hired, Lavoie was interviewed by Musk himself. "He's a very charming person when he wants something," Lavoie says. He wouldn't be drawn on Musk's politics - "that's his business" - but is unreserved about the company: "I've always been happily supportive and impressed, and would work hard with those incredible people again."Some analysts value SpaceX at less than half its current stock market price, warning  its ties to xAI carry real financial risk - part of a broader worry on Wall Street that sky-high valuations for AI-linked firms, including SpaceX, OpenAI and Anthropic, could prove overdone.Sinead O'Sullivan, an economist who has previously worked for Nasa, told the BBC in June she thinks SpaceX is an "Elon Musk ego project"."You're buying a share of the Elon Musk brand more than any kind of space industry," she said.But Ron Epstein, an aerospace analyst at Bank of America Securities, says the recent share price swings say more about the market than the company. "A lot of it has to do with macro trends," he says. "None of it really has anything to do with what's going on fundamentally at the company."He says investors judging SpaceX purely as an AI bet are missing the point: "They're not just a compute provider. They're not just an AI company. It's a far more complicated picture than that."SpaceX, he adds, has cut the cost of reaching orbit from around $10,000-$20,000 a kilogram to about $2,000 with its Falcon 9 rocket - "they have built a railroad to space."Lavoie, for his part, isn't rattled. He says: "The solid business model of SpaceX will prove itself to be worth the investment,"even as he takes some of his own winnings off the table.

schema.headline: Cashing in on SpaceX: 'Every chance I get, I'll sell a little more'

title: Meta becomes latest firm to say its AI hacked another company
description: Facebook owner Meta has become the latest tech firm to say one of its AI models was able to connect to the internet and hack into another organisation
body: Facebook owner Meta has become the latest tech firm to say one of its AI models was able to connect to the internet and hack into another organisation's systems, during testing.The incident, which Meta says occurred during an evaluation by an independent company, is the fourth recent incident of its kind disclosed by AI companies.Similar breaches by OpenAI and Anthropic models have raised cyber-security concerns and prompted calls for tougher safeguards and more rigorous testing.A Meta spokesperson told the BBC that it was investigating the hack, which it said had been caused by a "misconfiguration" by its independent tester.It also described what happened as similar to previously reported incidents at other firms.Meta said the security trials were conducted by Irregular, the same AI security vendor that carried out tests for Anthropic's AI model that had gained access to three other companies' systems.An Irregular spokesperson said the Meta incident "is the exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week."Irregular is working on a report on how to securely run cyber-security tests involving AI agents, the firm's spokesperson told the BBC.Meta also said it will publish more information on the incident "once we have all the facts."In the past two weeks, AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic have also reported incidents in which their models hacked into other organisation's systems during testing.ChatGPT-maker OpenAI said in a series of announcements that its agents attacked several publicly available services, including AI tools hub Hugging Face.OpenAI's disclosure prompted rival Anthropic to conduct its own checks, leading to the discovery that its Claude AI model had carried out similar attacks on several firms after a "misconfiguration" gave it access to the internet.  Daniel Hulme, global chief AI officer of advertising firm WPP, told the BBC that such AI models "are not conscious — they're not deliberately doing something devious"."What they're doing is coming up with very sophisticated strategies or cyberattacks to be able to achieve the goal that they've been given," he told the Today programme."When you give an AI a goal, if you don't think of all the ways it might be able to achieve the goal, it will find a way to achieve a goal that you haven't thought about."

schema.headline: Meta becomes latest firm to say its AI hacked another company

title: Afghan boxer accused of killing Scottish aid worker returns to court
description: An Afghan boxer suspected of killing a Scottish woman in Greece has arrived in court in Athens for a second time.Sharif Ahmadzai, who is 26 and from A
body: An Afghan boxer suspected of killing a Scottish woman in Greece has arrived in court in Athens for a second time.Sharif Ahmadzai, who is 26 and from Afghanistan, faces charges of homicide with intent, robbery and weapons offences.He is accused of killing aid worker Elisabeth Ross, 38, who was discovered by a homeless man in a derelict building in the Kypseli area of the Greek capital on July 18.Ahmadzai arrived back in court in Athens on Thursday morning in an unmarked Grey car. He was not pictured. It is expected he will be formally charged later.On Wednesday, he was assigned a court-appointed lawyer and given time to prepare his defence.Ahmadzai was initially detained on illegal weapons possession charges and is facing a charge of homicide with intent, as well as allegations that he stole more than €10,000 (£8,500) from the victim's bank accounts using her bank cards. Homicide with intent is equivalent to a murder charge in Scots law.A statement from the police's organised crime directorate said Ahmadzai was brought to a police station on 30 July. "In particular, it emerged that the 26-year-old placed the body in a suitcase and transported it to the abandoned site," the statement said.

schema.headline: Afghan boxer accused of killing Scottish aid worker returns to court

title: Meredith Kercher's sister criticises Amanda Knox Edinburgh Festival Fringe show
description: The sister of Meredith Kercher has criticised a solo comedy show by Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering her British roomma
body: The sister of Meredith Kercher has criticised a solo comedy show by Amanda Knox, who was convicted and later acquitted of murdering her British roommate in Italy in 2007. The Edinburgh Festival Fringe website says Knox's show, Cartwheel, is about motherhood and how she will explain what happened in Perugia to her daughter. Stephanie Kercher, addressing Knox directly on BBC Breakfast, said: "What I would say [to Knox] is to think about the family here, think about her friends and to turn the tables if it was your sister that this had happened to, because I know you have a sister as well."A spokesperson for Knox said the show, set to run over 11 days from Friday, honours Kercher's memory. Her comedy show's title Cartwheel references a story that once claimed she did cartwheels in the police station after her friend's death.Knox told the Telegraph newspaper, external last week: "I don't joke about Meredith's death. I joke a lot about how I was vilified, but I don't joke about her murder."Asked if Meredith Kercher would have found her comedy funny, she added: "Yeah, I think so. I mean, it is funny!".Responding to that suggestion, Stephanie Kercher told the BBC: "Meredith absolutely wouldn't find these topics of any comedy value."She said: "Our family's pain is immense. I can't explain to you how much pain our family have been through, and also we're talking two decades later now, this pain."A petition against the show, set up by a friend of Meredith, has been signed by just over 2,400 people, and says the show disrespects her memory and also risks normalising violence against women by making light of such a harrowing event. Referencing the petition, Stephanie Kercher told BBC Breakfast: "It's not just our family that feels this pain, and I do think this is something that needs to be looked at, because it sets a precedent for anyone else to do a show like this."She urged Prime Minister Andy Burnham to explore the issue and said she would like to meet him. "I think that if it was a generic theme, as many comedy shows are, even when they're pushing the boundaries, it would be different," she added."Because this is associated with an individual case and individual person, I think that's where the worry lies here for me, because who else is this going to then open up this opportunity for."The venue for the show next week, the Gilded Balloon Teviot, said Edinburgh Festival Fringe provides a platform for a wide range of voices in line with the commitment to freedom of expression. Since Meredith Kercher's death, Knox has written two books about her imprisonment and served as an executive producer on the biographical drama The Twisted Tale of Amanda Knox. Now 39, she is married with two children and lives in Washington state.Knox, from Seattle in the US, and Meredith Kercher, from Surrey in the UK, were both language exchange students sharing a house in the university town of Perugia.Alongside her then-boyfriend, Raffaele Sollecito, Knox was arrested on suspicion of murdering Kercher, 21, who was found dead in their house. Her throat had been cut and she had been sexually assaulted.After being found guilty, Knox served four years in an Italian prison before she and Sollecito were acquitted through an appeal. She returned home to the US in 2011.A retrial in 2014 reinstated Knox and Sollecito's convictions but Italy's top appeals court finally overturned their convictions in 2015.Ivory Coast-born Rudy Guede served 13 years of a 16-year sentence for Kercher's murder after his fingerprints were found at the scene.The court ruled that he did not act alone, but after Knox and Sollecito were acquitted no other accomplices were convicted.

schema.headline: Meredith Kercher's sister criticises Amanda Knox Edinburgh Festival Fringe show

title: Iran says deal with Oman on Strait of Hormuz is 'in final stages'
description: Iran says it has reached an agreement with Oman on a route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei did not
body: Iran says it has reached an agreement with Oman on a route for shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.Foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei did not give any further details on the agreement, which he said was "in the final stages".Baqaei warned, however, that a deal with Oman would not guarantee safe navigation through the strait, arguing security remained impacted by the US blockade of Iran's ports. The US and Oman have not commented on the proposal.Since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, Tehran has largely blocked the Strait of Hormuz through which about a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas usually passes.On Tuesday, US President Donald Trump warned that Iran would be "hit very hard" if the strait did not open "very soon".His comments came after senior US officials said talks had progressed to allow shipments to potentially resume later this week, though Iran has maintained that it is not negotiating with the US and has no plans to do so.Reopening the strait has been a key point in discussions between the two countries and mediators.In his statement, the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman said the "geographical coordinates of the route" had been agreed with Oman."The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States, particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," he said, according to Iran's official Irna news agency.Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi later told Irna the new route would be temporary and could stay open from two to four months. He did not give further details.Oil prices edged lower on Thursday, with global benchmark Brent crude down by 0.3% at $79.24 (£58.84) in morning Asian trade. Energy prices have fluctuated wildly during the conflict as shipments through the key route for around 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) have been severely disrupted.Since the beginning of the war, traffic through the strait has dwindled. Iran has said all passage needs to be cleared beforehand - and it has attacked vessels which have ignored the order.One of the main points of disagreement between Tehran and Washington has been Iran's threat to impose a fee on vessels wishing to cross the strait. Iran is seeking fees of between 5% and 7% of the price of cargoes from ships using the strait, according to a senior Iranian official cited by Reuters. Oman is discussing fees of around 3%, while Washington wants no fees at all.The proposed deal would also give Tehran control over ships entering the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, Reuters reported.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.In June, Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), aiming to stop fighting, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and reach agreement to end the war within 60 days.The deal quickly fell through, as did diplomatic talks, with tit-for-tat attacks resuming just days after the MoU was signed.The US has maintained a naval blockade of Iranian ports in the region, while another blockade is in place on Saudi Arabia's ports in the Red Sea, imposed by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis since 20 July.The US and Israel launched wide-ranging strikes on Iran on 28 February, with Iran responding by attacking Israel and US-allied states in the Gulf, and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz. Iran's then Supreme Leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, was killed in that first attack, after which he was succeeded by his son Mojtaba Khamenei.The younger Khamenei was wounded in the same strikes that launched the war and has not appeared in public since.Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Wednesday that communication with Khamenei was "difficult at the moment"."In any case, his presence is a very great source of strength for us so that we can continue," Pezeshkian said, according to state media.The younger Khamenei, who did not appear at his father's funeral ceremonies last month, has communicated through written statements but his low profile has led to speculation about his relations with other top officials.Pezeshkian insisted he had been able to hold productive meetings with him and been met with "kindness and very sound logic"."Unfortunately, the current situation allows some malicious people to describe him differently and to present a different image of him," he said.

schema.headline: Iran says deal with Oman on Strait of Hormuz is 'in final stages'

title: Sunshine to meal times: How to beat jet lag
description: Jet lag is what you feel when local time changes abruptly, but your body clock is playing catch up, says Dr Nina Rzechorzek, who leads research at the
body: Jet lag is what you feel when local time changes abruptly, but your body clock is playing catch up, says Dr Nina Rzechorzek, who leads research at the University of Cambridge on human brain temperature, sleep, and circadian rhythms."After rapid travel across several time zones, your internal biological time initially stays aligned with home while you are trying to sleep, eat, and function on destination time."That mismatch can cause disturbed sleep, daytime sleepiness, poor concentration, irritability, reduced performance, and digestive problems," she says.And jet lag is closely linked to what are called our circadian rhythms – the body's internal body clock."Almost all the cells in our body maintain their own 24-hour clock, which are synchronised by a master clock in the brain," explains Dr Anna Edmondson, of the Laboratory of Molecular Biology at the University of Cambridge."The master clock is set to environmental timing cues, one of the most important cues being daily cycles in sunlight and darkness. However, if the timing of the sunlight/darkness cycles suddenly change (you fly far east or west), then it takes several days for the master clock to adjust to the new time, leading to jet lag."So effectively, it's like your body is still stuck in the timezone of where you've just flown from."

schema.headline: Sunshine to meal times: How to beat jet lag

title: In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strike campaign
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russian missiles and drones are hammering Ukraine's Black Sea ports, like OdesaByPaul AdamsDiplomatic corresp
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Russian missiles and drones are hammering Ukraine's Black Sea ports, like OdesaByPaul AdamsDiplomatic correspondent in Odesa"My crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also died."Svitlana Halchenko winces as she remembers the Russian ballistic missile which exploded at work in Odesa, killing her colleagues. Svitlana works as a warehouse shift manager at the city's main port.Despite her injuries – she walks with a limp, pieces of shrapnel still embedded in her leg and back – Svitlana is determined to keep working.But her normally bustling workplace is largely silent.Russia is ramping up its efforts to strangle Ukraine's commercial links to the outside world, launching attacks all along the country's Black Sea coastline.From damaged port infrastructure to listing ships with bridges blackened and containers still smouldering, the evidence is everywhere. Nowhere more so than out towards the horizon, where the approaches to Ukraine's once bustling ports – Odesa, Chornomorsk, Pivdennyi – are almost devoid of ships.Svitlana maintains a brave smile throughout our conversation, but her distress is painfully obvious. Her fingers constantly twist a tissue as she tries to maintain her composure and she gazes into the distance as tears well up behind her glasses.The last few weeks have been worse than ever."It's been very difficult for morale," she says with a deep sigh. "A lot of sirens, a lot of shaheds [drones], a lot of hits. People are very tense."Maarten Lernout/BBCMy crane operator, my partner, died five metres from me… The driver remained in the cabin. He also diedAccording to Ukraine's port administration, July saw 57 Russian attacks on civilian vessels, 22 of them at sea, and a further 67 hits on port infrastructure.While there have been Russian attacks on international vessels before, they've never been so numerous or so deadly.On July 19, a Turkish-owned cargo vessel, Golden Leo, was struck by three Russian missiles, killing nine Indian and Syrian crew members and a Ukrainian pilot.The ship, carrying Ukrainian corn, sank off Odesa a week later.According to the global shipping journal Lloyd's List, the Black Sea may now be the most dangerous place for shipping in the world - with July the deadliest month for merchant seamen, external since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began. At his union's offices in the port city, Oleg Grygoriuk, Chairman of the Marine Transport Workers Union of Ukraine, says his members are suffering."There are a lot of veterans who already served their country," he says, "and they literally say that being in the port is more scary than being on the front line."Odesa's proximity to Russian-occupied territory means that workers often have little time to react."A missile flies from Crimea within a minute," he says. "If you are sitting in a crane, you need three and a half minutes to get down and go to the shelter. There's literally no time to do that."On a rare visit to one of the area's main ports, we saw almost no sign of movement. Hundreds of metres of berths sat empty and towering gantry cranes stood idle as a skeleton crew conducted maintenance.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Odesa's port lies empty now as Russia steps up its attacksThe military authorities allowed the visit on strict condition that we neither name the facility nor film anything. Ukraine doesn't want Russia to know what has and hasn't been damaged or reveal details that might aid Moscow in further targeting.Two damaged cargo vessels were moored nearby. Both had suffered severe damage to the superstructure, where the bridge and crew quarters are located.Just one lone freighter was seen moving towards the port."My heart is broken," a senior manager told us on condition we didn't name him."Normally there's a queue, even out at sea, waiting for a berth.""There was a deal," he said, referring to the UN-brokered 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports. The agreement established safe maritime corridors to Odesa's main ports."They stopped the deal in the middle of 2023, but they didn't start attacking it until recently," the manager said."Today they do it systematically."Halfway through our tour, sirens sounded, forcing us to seek shelter for several minutes as a Russian jet-powered drone flew overhead.Weary dock workers scanned their phones for updates until the all-clear sounded.The manager said recent alerts have forced the port to shut down for 15 out of 24 hours.Technically, the port is open, as are all the others in the area. There is no prohibition on commercial ships attempting to use them. But the risks are clearly too great for most shipowners."There is barely anybody who wants to call because there is a huge problem with people getting killed," says Andrey Stavnitser, co-owner and CEO of one of the largest ports in the area."We can see that the whole supply chain is on hold."Image caption, Russia has made Ukraine's Black Sea coastline incredibly dangerous for shippingStavnitser says Russia is almost certainly retaliating for Ukraine's recent, highly successful attacks on Russian shipping, including sanctioned vessels carrying oil, as well as other ships involved in ferrying supplies to Russian-occupied Crimea.Using its own drones, Ukraine's Operation MoLoChKa (which roughly translates as "Moscow will fall through Crimea") has struck around 200 Russian vessels, bringing traffic in the strategic Sea of Azov to a virtual standstill.Ukrainians bristle at the suggestion that Russia and Ukraine are playing the same game. Kyiv is attempting to loosen Moscow's grip on occupied territory, they point out, while Russia is preventing Ukraine from exporting badly needed grain to the international market.With Ukraine's summer grain harvest well under way, this is all happening at the worst possible time."It's the most sensitive period," says Volodymyr Slavinskyi, trading director for Nibulon, one of the country's leading grain exporters."Farmers need to quickly harvest grains from the fields, not to lose the crop. They need to be able to sell the crop they harvested and reinvest money in the next production cycle."The impact of a prolonged shutdown of Ukraine's ports are likely to be severe. Ukraine is one of the world's largest producers of grain and oilseeds, supplying around 6% of global wheat exports before Russia's full-scale invasion and 10% of corn exports. But reports suggest, external its export capacity has dropped by at least a third since Russia launched its full-scale invasion.The Black Sea remains a vital export route for the country. Last year, the Greater Odesa ports accounted for more than 73 million tonnes of Ukraine's maritime exports, with grain accounting for 38 million tonnes.With almost no vessels currently moving on Ukraine's Black Sea shipping corridor, traders are already counting the cost of this summer's closure."I would say we've already lost the ability to deliver to global customers around half a million or 700,000 metric tons of Ukrainian grains and oilseeds," Slavinskyi says.Image source, Kristina Volk/BBCImage caption, Volodymyr Slavinskyi says Ukraine has lost a huge amount of its export capacityAway from the port, Odesa is determined to show off a very different side. The summer season is in full swing. The beaches are packed as visitors descend on the Black Sea from all over Ukraine.Buskers perform on the city's famous Potemkin Stairs, while sunbathers barely flinch as the sirens sound and explosions rumble in the distance.In a video published on Monday, swimmers were seen removing a Russian drone from the water as holidaymakers look on.They know the risks. In late June, 26-year-old Daria Kravchenko was killed when shrapnel from an intercepted Russian drone landed on the beach.This week, holidaymakers on Russia's equally Black Sea coast suffered a similar fate when an intercepted Ukrainian drone crashed onto a busy beach.Local authorities said seven people were killed, including three children.It's not clear what Ukraine was targeting, but this war on ships and ports has many casual victims. Sailors, dockworkers or people simply unlucky enough to live or work nearby.Outside Odesa, after a recent drone explosion, we found 83-year-old Andrii Dudik, surveying the mangled wreckage of his house and garden.He was physically unscathed and remarkably sanguine about the drone that had shattered his routine afternoon nap just hours earlier."I was lying there, wondering what I was going to do this afternoon. Now I know," he joked.Did he feel like an accidental victim of Russia's attacks on the nearby ports, I asked him."Absolutely," he replied. "And I won't forget it."Additional reporting by Kristina Volk, Anastasiia Levchenko and Joshua Cheetham

schema.headline: In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strike campaign

title: The 'education gap' hiding in picture-perfect Cornwall and Devon
description: This year, millions of holidaymakers will head to Cornwall and Devon for their sandy beaches and pretty coastal towns - just two reasons why the South
body: This year, millions of holidaymakers will head to Cornwall and Devon for their sandy beaches and pretty coastal towns - just two reasons why the South West peninsula is England's top tourist destination.Yet behind its wild coastal beauty and affluent towns lies a different story: one of lost opportunities and the unfulfilled potential of many growing up in the region.On almost every measure, the region is among the weakest educationally, according to the South West Social Mobility Commission, a coalition of organisations trying to bring about change.Disparities in GCSE results are often framed through the lens of a North-South divide, but that narrative can obscure the challenges facing children in coastal and rural parts of England.When you look at the regional data for English and maths GCSE passes for all pupils in England, you can see that, overall, the South outperforms the North.Tanya Ovenden-Hope, Professor of Education at Plymouth Marjon University, describes what happens in the South West as "pretty poverty", and says this leads to fewer young people reaching their full potential.She calls growing up in a low-income family in a coastal rural community a potentially "toxic" combination.The government does measure the level of disadvantage in communities but Prof Ovenden-Hope says too much of that is done using measures that work for towns and cities, including transport."If you live in Cornwall you have to own a car. It's not a luxury, it's a necessity, because everything you do and everywhere you go involves some kind of travel.  That's not measured by the government's measures of deprivation."This matters because it helps decide how government money is allocated across England."It's not all ice creams and sandy beaches and turquoise seas," says Dominic Wilkes, a headteacher who moved from Greater Manchester to Bude in North Cornwall.Higher housing costs and the need for a car impact training and teacher recruitment. While the remoteness of some communities can also act as a deterrent for young teachers to move here from other parts of England, according to recent research.For Wilkes, who works at the only secondary school in Bude, the main upside is better teacher retention, which helps build a deep connection to the local community.But inspiring children to think about different options for their future comes with its challenges.As a teacher in Greater Manchester, Wilkes could hop on a tram to take pupils to museums and different workplaces, including the BBC at MediaCity in Salford, as part of the curriculum. The nearest railway station is about 30 miles from Budehaven Community School. Pupils travel in from scattered villages and the area offers a relatively limited range of employers able to broaden their horizons or spark ambitions beyond the classroom.Year 10 pupil Ethan, from Budehaven Community School, wants to become a marine biologist and recently completed a work experience placement at a seal sanctuary that was a three-hour round trip by car."I love being in the sea and just protecting its habitats and wildlife, it really makes me excited to do something like that," he said."I think Cornwall's amazing and all my family are here but I think I want to be able to grow as a person. I think I can only do that by leaving and exploring new adventures."Year 9 student Burt told us he had to travel to Oxfordshire and Coventry to take part in the National Youth Choir, which meant his dad had to book a hotel to break up the journey.He thinks there are good opportunities to be found but they're more difficult, and sometimes costly, to access from his town.But others told us Cornwall is the perfect location for them. Poppy wants to be a florist and dreams of opening a seasonal business selling homegrown local wildflowers.Wilkes has decided to spend above average on careers advice and trips, including to universities, to help expand pupils' horizons but it is still hard.He had to turn down an offer of work experience from a "brilliant company" because although it didn't look too far on a map, it was five hours each way by road, without a direct bus service.This kind of challenge potentially deepens the divide between families who have the money to afford petrol for long-distance trips or holidays abroad, and those who are just about managing the basics with a rising cost of living.In the South West, much of the local employment is in farming or tourism, with young adults looking to leave and build their careers elsewhere.In 2024, jobs related to the visitor economy made up approximately 20% of employment in Cornwall.The South West Social Mobility Commission has other concerns about children who receive free school meals in the region.It warns that 46% of secondary pupils (and 27% of primary pupils) are persistently absent, which means missing 10% of their school time.While suspensions, exclusions and home education are also among the highest in England "raising important questions about school engagement, belonging and access to education".In young adulthood, the potential impact can be seen in the proportion who go on to university, one of the biggest long-term drivers of improved earnings and life chances between generations.In the South West, 19% of those who grew up receiving free school meals go on to get a degree, the lowest level in England, and below the North East. The national average is 29%.This is what motivated Nick Wakeling, a teacher at Colyton Grammar School, to get in touch.He runs the Colyton Foundation, a charity that supports young people into university.One of the foundation's schemes is Your Future Story, backed by schools and universities to support 1,000 secondary school pupils from lower income families through to university with targeted support.Libby is now considering a creative degree after Your Future Story arranged for her to go on a trip to Falmouth, a 1 hour 40 minute drive away. It "gave me an idea of what university would be like," she says.There is a big push for locally generated solutions from the South West Social Mobility Commission, funded by a coalition including Exeter University, which warns the region is near the bottom on most measures of educational attainment from early childhood onwards.While this can limit life chances in terms of getting to higher earnings, fewer young people in the South West are not in education, employment or training than most other parts of England. This is at a time when the national concern about what are called NEETs has reached an all-time high.The report found the South West has the highest proportion of people who received free school meals as children in sustained work by the age of 28.A Department for Education Spokesperson said: "This government believes every child should grow up with opportunity on their doorstep and hope for the future, with an education system that opens doors and cuts the link between background and success."From this September, two pilot projects on raising education results in coastal areas are getting under way in Hastings and Scarborough in what the government is calling Mission Coastal.The hope is to find approaches that transfer elsewhere, but the more rural and coastal South West may need to find quite different solutions.Additional reporting by Isobel Cottam and Libby Rogers.

schema.headline: The 'education gap' hiding in picture-perfect Cornwall and Devon

title: Shorts, strappy tops, sandals: Should you wear them in the office?
description: Shorts, strappy tops and sandals: What is acceptable to wear in the office?Image source, Getty ImagesByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Yet another summer
body: Shorts, strappy tops and sandals: What is acceptable to wear in the office?Image source, Getty ImagesByYasmin RufoBusiness reporter Yet another summer heatwave could be on the way to make your commute sweaty and your workplace stuffy.What to wear to work in the summer can be a surprisingly difficult decision. Shorts, strappy tops and sandals may keep you cool - but will they be judged too casual, revealing or unprofessional?There's a bare-legged backlash in Tokyo where officials encouraged men to swap suits for shorts at work, prompting complaints about hairy legs in the office.So what is acceptable to wear to work, how can you successfully style your summer wardrobe and can your boss tell you what you can and can't wear?Figure caption, Should men be allowed to wear shorts in the office?Conor, who works in media, has regularly worn shorts to the office during the recent hot weather. "Who gives a monkey's what you wear?" he says. "If you're able to do your job safely, professionally and appropriately, there's a lot to be said for letting people be comfortable."And many seem to agree - a recent poll by market research firm Ipsos found 62% of adults thought it was acceptable for men to wear shorts to work in hot weather, while 63% said the same for women.But we aren't talking short-shorts or denim hot pants fashion designer Amanda Wakeley points out: "If you're asking yourself whether they're too short, they probably are".She says shorts are "the trickiest item to get right in a professional environment" and recommends tailored, longer shorts paired with a crisp shirt or lightweight blazer for both men and women.Stylist Clare Chambers agrees shorts should sit around the kneecap for both men and women. For men, she recommends tailored chino-style shorts with an untucked T-shirt or shirt.Sandals Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Socks and sandals are a combo hard to pull off at the best of times, let alone in the officeWakeley describes flip-flops as one of the few definite "no" items in most offices. "They instantly signal leisure rather than professionalism and can make even the most polished outfit feel underdressed," she says.Chambers agrees, and says even during the hottest weather, woven flats are a better option because they are breathable while still covering the foot.Almost two-thirds of people questioned by Ipsos said they were unacceptable for men in the workplace, while 58% said the same for women.Sandals, however, are a slightly different matter as Wakeley says refined leather sandals can be entirely acceptable in many offices, provided they are clean and well maintained.The difference, she says, is whether they look like part of a considered outfit or something that would normally be worn around a swimming pool.She adds that while socks and sandals have become a viral fashion trend "it's important to consider whether a trend aligns with the image you want to communicate professionally". "This combination can read as highly casual and youthful, which may unintentionally detract from giving you a credible and authoritative presence."Strappy topsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Public opinion is divided over bare shoulders at workSome 40% of adults considered tank tops or vest tops acceptable for women at work, compared with only 24% who said the same for men, according to Ipsos.Natasia, a teacher in London, says at a previous school she and other staff had been summoned "regularly in the summer months to tell us off about our outfits."She says she was also told to cover up her tattoos. "It should be OK to have your arms out at work especially when it's hot," she says.Wakeley says a well-cut camisole or strappy top can work when worn beneath a linen overshirt, lightweight jacket or tailored co-ord. On its own, however, it may feel too informal.Chambers says if you're wearing a strappy top "you must wear a strapless bra as it utterly kills an outfit when you can see bra straps".She explains that thicker straps are a safer option where the dress code is unclear and recommends satin camisoles as a more polished alternative to basic cotton vests.She adds that while bandeau tops are "such an on-trend look this summer, they are a no-go for work"."The constant need to keep fiddling to pull them up displays an uncomfortable and unconfident demeanour," she says.How to style summer clothes at workImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The answer to dressing for the heat isn't necessarily to wear less, but to choose clothes more carefullyWakeley and Chambers both say that you don't need to lose your personal style when dressing for the office and you can still inject plenty of personality while following a dress code. Here are their top tips on how to style summer clothes for the office. Can your employer tell you what to wear?Climate change is expected to bring more severe, frequent and longer-lasting heatwaves in UK summers in the coming years.Employers are allowed to set standards around clothing and appearance, particularly where there are legitimate reasons such as safety, branding or maintaining a professional image.But employment lawyer Sarah Tahamtani says dress codes should be "reasonable, proportionate and capable of justification"."During extreme heat, employers should consider whether existing requirements remain practical and whether greater flexibility can be introduced."They must also consider employees with disabilities, medical conditions or other vulnerabilities that may be worsened by high temperatures.An employee who believes a request is unreasonable or inconsistently applied should first raise the issue with a manager or HR and explain how the rule is affecting their comfort or ability to work safely.

schema.headline: Shorts, strappy tops, sandals: Should you wear them in the office?

title: Raleigh's parent company starts insolvency proceedings
description: Raleigh was founded in Nottingham in 1887 and at one stage was the biggest bicycle maker in the world, employing about 8,000 people at its peak.It sto
body: Raleigh was founded in Nottingham in 1887 and at one stage was the biggest bicycle maker in the world, employing about 8,000 people at its peak.It stopped making bikes in the city decades ago, and in 2024 it vacated its headquarters on Church Street in Eastwood to move to new premises less than a mile away.Announcing plans to initiate insolvency proceedings, Nilsson said Accell had worked "to restructure [its] operations and finances"."Every realistic option for the future of the business has been tirelessly explored, and none have resulted in a solution to continue the group in its current form," he said."Our immediate focus is to support an orderly process, provide clarity wherever possible, and work with the relevant court-appointed administrators to preserve viable activities and employment where circumstances allow."

schema.headline: Raleigh's parent company starts insolvency proceedings

title: PC Harper widow 'will not give up' opposing early releases
description: PC Harper widow 'won't give up' early release fightImage source, Martis MediaImage caption, Lissie Harper successfully campaigned for harsher sentence
body: PC Harper widow 'won't give up' early release fightImage source, Martis MediaImage caption, Lissie Harper successfully campaigned for harsher sentences for the manslaughter of emergency workers on dutyByDave GilyeatSouth of EnglandThe widow of a police officer has said she hopes people will share a petition calling for his killers to be denied early release from prison, insisting she "will not give up".PC Andrew Harper, from Wallingford, died in 2019 when he was dragged by a car as three teenagers fled the scene of a Berkshire quad bike theft.Under updated plans to tackle prison overcrowding, two of PC Harper's killers - Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers - would be eligible for release next year.Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the government was trying to avert "a prison capacity crisis".Lissie Harper said: "Hopefully we can make the current government come to their senses and realise we cannot put people like this back on our streets."Justice should mean justice and serving the sentence given."As of just after 08:30 BST, the petition had over 440,000 signatures. It was started by Aileen O'Connor, chair of Thames Valley Police Federation.Image source, Martis MediaImage caption, Police officer Andrew Harper suffered fatal injuries while on duty in 2019Cole and Bowers were each sentenced to 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, and will become eligible for release after serving half of their sentences.The driver of the vehicle, Henry Long, received a 16-year sentence and will not be eligible.On Monday, the government announced revised plans that would exclude prisoners who had committed rape, grooming, and serious child sex offences from an early release scheme for England and Wales.But people guilty of manslaughter are still eligible for earlier release.O'Connor told the BBC the news was "having a huge impact on morale".She added: "Lissie Harper, [PC Harper's] parents, his brother, his family, his close friends - they are serving the life sentence of not having Andrew Harper here today fulfilling his best potential for his life."Image caption, Aileen O'Connor is chair of the Thames Valley Police FederationIn the wake of PC Harper's death, Lissie Harper campaigned for harsher sentences for the manslaughter of emergency workers on duty.Harper's Law was among the new measures in the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act.It means that, if convicted today, his killers would not be eligible for the early release scheme.In a statement, Lissie said: "Seven years later, we are now faced with a secondary gut punch that is coming from our own government."The sentences Andrew's killers received were pitiful - and the fact we are hearing these absurd reasons for early release like prisons being too full is disgraceful and disgusting."The people making these decisions should be utterly ashamed of themselves."'Prison crisis'The government said it was trying to avoid running out of prison spaces as soon as October this year.The justice secretary said about 1,000 prisoners would now not be released early following the revision to the scheme."If we drew it any wider we would have a prison capacity crisis," Alex Norris said.Prisoners released on licence, he said, would be subject to "very significant controls on their lives" and victims would be consulted.But Olivia Bailey, the Labour MP for the Reading and Mid West constituency, said: "PC Harper's killers should not be eligible for early release, and I am deeply disappointed that the government have not exempted them from the early release scheme following their review."I will continue to do whatever I can to challenge this decision."Get in touchYour Voice

schema.headline: PC Harper widow 'will not give up' opposing early releases

title: Are AI recruitment tools affecting mid-life women's careers?
description: 'I've had to Botox my CV': Are AI recruitment tools affecting women's careers?Image caption, Stacey Duguid believes AI-powered recruitment tools are d
body: 'I've had to Botox my CV': Are AI recruitment tools affecting women's careers?Image caption, Stacey Duguid believes AI-powered recruitment tools are disadvantaging mid-life womenByLondon work and money correspondentUpdated 48 minutes agoThe fear of becoming surplus to requirements because of advancements in AI is one shared by millions of workers, but are AI recruitment tools posing a specific threat to women trying to return to employment?After a career spanning decades, with senior corporate roles in fashion, and a period of freelancing, 52-year-old Stacey Duguid decided to find "one last job". What followed was 16 months of sending "gazillions" of CVs, with little more than a handful of automated replies, despite never previously struggling to find work.Feeling "lonely and shameful" and wondering if it was a "me problem", she posted on social media asking whether other women her age were having the same experience. The response was overwhelming, with thousands of women saying they were facing similar struggles.Stacey, who lives in north London, believes AI-powered recruitment tools could be contributing to the problem and has "Botoxed" her CV by removing references to her age and experience."AI holds a mirror up to society. It's a reflection of our bias," she said."I'm not saying this is just a women's issue; I've had messages from men too. My point is about gendered ageism."Confidence 'taken a hit'The BBC has since spoken to more than 60 women aged 40 to 65 across a range of industries who have been struggling to find work.Most have decades of experience in senior roles and say they've submitted countless CVs, only to receive automated rejections or no response at all.Like Stacey, many believe AI recruitment tools are playing a role. Image source, Koeyli JalukaImage caption, Koeyli Jaluka says that after applying for more than 400 jobs, her confidence has "taken a hit"Koeyli Jaluka, 49, has held senior roles across manufacturing, corporate and healthcare."I've never been in this position before. For the last 10–12 years I've been headhunted. Now I'm hunting for jobs and being relentlessly rejected."Made redundant nine months ago, she's applied for 442 jobs and has heard back in only a few cases. She's occasionally been told she's "too senior" – which she believes is "code for old". Despite two decades of experience and two degrees, she says her confidence has "taken a hit".She believes tighter budgets, AI screening and increasingly narrow hiring criteria are all contributing."A lot of us have been told by career coaches to shave off the first 10 years of work on our CVs just to ensure we don't come across as having worked for too long."'I'm on jobseeker's allowance'Image source, Anna CowieImage caption, Anna Cowie says she's lost count of the number of CVs she's sentAnna Cowie, 52, had a 30-year career in advertising but has been unemployed for almost four years. She's lost count of the number of CVs she's sent, despite having never previously been without a job.After decades of working for big brands, most recently helping to launch the new Battersea Power Station, she's now on jobseeker's allowance. Anna has turned to volunteering for community festivals, and has found networking with real people a much more promising approach."You're seen as a human and not just lines on paper."'Huge repercussions'While it is impossible to know in many cases whether AI tools played a role in a screening or a rejection because employers rarely disclose details of their recruitment processes, there are widespread fears that AI recruitment tools are disadvantaging mid-life women, external.The City of London Women Pivoting to Digital Taskforce, which focuses on women in the financial and professional services sector, has raised concerns, external about the growing use of AI in recruitment and its impact on women.Chair Caroline Haines said the taskforce's research found significant concern that AI used to screen job applications and CVs does not recognise the skills many experienced women can bring.Image caption, Caroline Haines says there is concern that AI used in recruitment does not account for many women's skills"There is a high level of concern that AI at initial recruitment level... doesn't account for the skills of a vast body of women that could be very effective and therefore promote economic growth," she said.For example, women who have taken time out of work for childcare may have gaps in their CVs that some AI screening systems could interpret negatively.In terms of the bigger picture, the taskforce estimates AI and automation could displace hundreds of thousands of women's jobs by 2035. Using data from Market and skills projections: 2020 to 2035, Department for Education, external, the taskforce estimates that without significant investment in retraining, firms could face more than £750m in severance costs.   In the digital taskforce's recent survey, external of over 1,000 women, 68% said they had not been given the opportunity by their employer to retrain or transition into digital roles."When the country is desperate for economic growth, we need to use whatever resource we have, and the resource of women who are mid-career, mid-experience. If they drop out of the market there are huge repercussions," Haines said.Image caption, Laura Holden believes AI recruitment tools have the potential to cause "significant harm" The BBC understands that some London-based companies have stopped using AI tools for fear of bias in their recruitment. Laura Holden, an AI lawyer and founder of the Bonsai AI and legal consultancy, said companies often do not understand how the tools work, which has the potential to cause "significant harm".She argued it is difficult to determine whether there is bias because "there is a lack of regulation globally that requires providers to show how their tools work".She pointed to CV screening tools and AI-scored interviews as examples of where bias can emerge.One tool, she said, grades CVs from A to D, encouraging recruiters to prioritise higher-ranked candidates. Others flag factors such as a seven-year career gap as a "thing to note", potentially influencing decisions unfairly.Holden said providers were "very quick" to claim their tools are safe and reduce bias, while designing and marketing them in ways that encourage employers to reject large numbers of applicants based on AI-generated scores. Although companies describe them as decision-support tools, she said they often functioned as "automated decision-making systems".She called for mandatory testing and stronger regulation before AI recruitment tools are deployed, arguing existing laws were not designed with AI in mind.'Completely faulty' logicDr Eleanor Drage, a senior researcher at the University of Cambridge, said concerns about AI disadvantaging women in recruitment are "very justified". She argued that human recruiters were better able to recognise the value of candidates returning from career breaks, such as maternity leave, and the transferable skills they bring - qualities AI may overlook. While Drage said it was "very difficult" to prove AI recruitment tools are inherently biased, she argued the logic they operate by is "completely faulty" because they cannot assess a person's intrinsic value or personality in the way a human recruiter could. Figure caption, Stacey Duguid appeared on Tuesday's Woman's HourShe added that many recruiters do not fully understand how these tools work, and said companies should use AI to evaluate their own hiring practices rather than to assess "vulnerable populations, like older women going back into the workforce, or people who've had a career break".While Drage acknowledges the benefits of using the tools, including helping hiring managers identify candidates with similar characteristics to people who have previously been hired, she says often "they're not on the side of the jobseeker".'Rigorously tested'The concerns raised in this article by interviewees relate to the use of AI-powered recruitment tools more broadly and are not directed at any single provider.Workday, the maker of popular AI-powered human resources software, is facing claims, external that it violated Californian law thousands of times by ​weeding out job applicants at many major companies for discriminatory reasons.The case is proceeding, with a ruling expected later this year.The BBC contacted Workday, which said the claims in the suit were false, adding that its tools don't make hiring decisions. More generally, Workday highlights that its recruitment tools help recruiters identify candidates who best match a job description based on their skills and experience, supporting rather than replacing human judgement.The company said its AI was "rigorously tested" through its Responsible AI programme and "does not consider traits such as age or gender".Workday added that, when used responsibly, AI can help qualified candidates avoid "getting lost in the pile".Image source, Eleanor DrageImage caption, AI recruitment tools are often "not on the side of the jobseeker", according to Dr Eleanor DragePrime Minister Andy Burnham recently raised concerns about AI used in hiring, and that it hadn't made "recruitment fairer". A government spokesperson said: "While AI can help employers manage large volumes of applications and reduce administrative burdens, it is vital that recruitment processes remain fair, transparent and accessible. "Existing legal protections, including equality and data protection law, already apply to AI systems, and we will act where additional protections are needed."A spokesperson for Mayor of London Sir Sadiq Khan said AI presented both opportunities and challenges, particularly as women are more likely to work in AI-exposed roles. They said the mayor had backed recommendations from the London AI and Jobs Taskforce to help employers adopt AI responsibly and support workers through the transition.As for Stacey, she has set up a community chat and platform to help women feel less alone, and to help companies address the issues in question."I want us, as a group, to be heard and seen. And for gendered ageism to become a thing of the past."Because if we're lucky, we all get old."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, X and Instagram. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.ukGet in touchHave you been affected by the issues in this story? Share your experiences

schema.headline: Are AI recruitment tools affecting mid-life women's careers?

title: Rihanna working on new music, says A$AP Rocky
description: Rihanna could be set to break a decade-long album hiatus, according to her partner A$AP Rocky."She in the studio right now," the rapper said on the Th
body: Rihanna could be set to break a decade-long album hiatus, according to her partner A$AP Rocky."She in the studio right now," the rapper said on the The Jason Lee podcast on Wednesday. Few details about the project were revealed, apart from a denial that the pair would collaborate on a double album. However, in response to questioning about about a potential new album, he added "she cooking."The singer and beauty mogul from Barbados, whose real name is Robyn Fenty, has not released a full album since 2016's Anti."Are you the reason we don't have an album?" podcaster Jason Lee asked the rapper on his show, noting the three children shared by the pair and Rihanna's travel.The rapper denied this, instead saying that the singer was in fact working on new music."Yeah I said it, sorry babe," he continued, adding that he would "get in trouble for this."Little other information about the possible music was revealed in the interview.In February last year, Rihanna said that she felt "really optimistic" about a new album. "I feel like I've finally cracked it, girl!," she told a reporter from Harper's Bazaar.She also said, "I cannot put up anything mediocre. After waiting eight years, you might as well just wait some more."Since her last album, Rihanna has released singles, including some linked to film projects, including 2022's Lift Me Up for Black Panther: Wakanda Forever. She has also launched multiple businesses, including her popular makeup range Fenty Beauty and a lingerie company. The 38-year-old's net worth has been estimated by Forbes at over a billion dollars.During the interview, A$AP Rocky, real name Rakim Mayers, refused to comment on whether he and Rihanna had married.

schema.headline: Rihanna working on new music, says A$AP Rocky

title: Majority of England's rivers and lakes fail pollution review
description: The government is already on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal
body: The government is already on course to miss its legally binding target of restoring 77% of England's waters to good ecological status by 2027 - a goal the environmental watchdog, the Office for Environmental Protection, has warned will be missed by a "considerable margin".It's now investigating both the government and the Environment Agency over possible rule breaches.Environment Secretary Angela Eagle said the figures "underline the need for wholesale change across the water sector".She pointed to new laws the government has introduced to hold water companies to account and record investment. "We will drive forward a system that puts the public interest first," she said.Much of the debate about the state of England's waters has centred on water companies and the sewage they release into rivers. But campaigners and scientists also point to agriculture as an equally large source of pollution - one that attracts far less public attention.Erica Popplewell, of the campaign group River Action, said some farming, particularly intensive poultry units - vast sheds housing hundreds of thousands of birds - were a growing threat to rivers such as the Wye and Severn."There's a lot of poo that comes out of the chickens," she said. "If it goes straight into a river, it causes eutrophication. The whole ecology of the river is damaged, and the river is dying." She called on the government to tackle sewage and farming "with the same urgency".The National Farmers' Union of England and Wales has been approached for comment.Other types of pollution affecting England's bodies of water, the Environment Agency pointed to, include petrol, garden pesticides and contaminated water running off roads picking up microplastics.The Environment Agency stressed that this year's data could not be directly compared with 2019 because it had changed its methods.In particular, it said the steep fall in the number of lakes ranked as good - down about half from 2019 - largely reflected a change in how its experts now assess them, rather than a genuine decline in their condition.Its chair, Alan Lovell, acknowledged too many water bodies were "still not achieving the standards we want to see", adding that the agency was "transforming our enforcement work" with its largest ever workforce.But Prof Penny Johnes, a leading water quality scientist at the University of Bristol, told BBC News the true picture was almost certainly worse than the classifications suggested.The scheme was "not fit for purpose", she said, measuring too few pollutants too infrequently, and missing nitrogen and other substances scientists have long understood to be driving rivers' decline.The findings come as much of England sits in official drought, with rivers running low and more than 20 million people facing hosepipe bans. Lower flows can concentrate the very pollution the new data is designed to track, leaving fish and other aquatic life exposed to more dangerous levels. Hundreds of dead fish linked to heatwave and pollutionClimate change is expected to bring drier and hotter summers which could further exacerbate this issue. Asked directly whether England's waters were healthier than six or seven years ago, Prof Johnes said: "No, definitely not."Every river and lake failed the test for chemical pollution.The Environment Agency said this is because legacy substances, such as heavy metals from mining, take decades to break down, and some are building up. But Prof Johnes said it was also a "failure to regulate effectively" the new chemicals entering rivers, from antibiotics to the "forever chemicals" known as PFAS - many not routinely monitored.There are currently 23 enforcement notices against water companies requiring them to lower the levels of PFAS to reduce the danger to human health.Water UK, which represents the water companies, has called for PFAS use to be banned to limit their build-up and reduce water treatment costs, but the chemicals are currently used in thousands of products, from school uniforms to medical devices.It said it was spending record amounts of money on improving the country's waterways."Water companies are investing £22bn in environmental improvements by 2030. This will help to secure our water supplies, support economic growth and end sewage entering our rivers and seas."The Environment Agency also noted that other European countries are doing even worse in terms of the good health of their waterways, with only 8% in Germany and just 1% in the Netherlands.But Prof Johnes said such a comparison is misleading, because of varying methodologies across nations.

schema.headline: Majority of England's rivers and lakes fail pollution review
